analysis.one_liner: Implements three international treaties restricting highly toxic, long-lasting pesticides and requiring notice of banned pesticide exports.
analysis.headline: The House Agriculture Committee approved the bill by voice vote in 2006, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write three international environmental agreements into U.S. pesticide law: the Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants, a related air-pollution protocol, and the Rotterdam Convention, which requires countries to be told before hazardous pesticides are exported to them. It prohibits sale or use of listed toxic pesticides in ways that violate the treaties, requires exporters of banned or restricted pesticides to notify the government before each shipment, and requires warning labels and safety sheets. It also sets up a public notice-and-comment process, with reports by the EPA, before any newly listed chemical triggers domestic restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to persistent toxic chemicals: the treaties target pesticides like DDT, aldrin, and chlordane that build up in the food chain and the environment. Farm communities, people living near application sites, and foreign importers who would finally receive formal notice when a pesticide banned in the U.S. is shipped to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities exposed to persistent toxic pesticides

how_it_helps.text: No person could sell, distribute, use, produce, or dispose of a listed POPs pesticide in a way inconsistent with U.S. obligations under the treaties [S4].

Exporters of pesticides banned or severely restricted in the U.S. would have to notify the EPA 15 to 45 days before export, and the EPA would pass the notice to the importing country's government, implementing the Rotterdam Convention's prior-informed-consensus procedure [S4].

Banned or restricted pesticides exported abroad would have to carry hazard labeling and safety data sheets, and the EPA would publish public notices about which pesticides are listed under the treaties and the status of any listing proposals [S4].
The EPA would have to publish periodic public reports on the status of chemicals proposed for international listing, giving the public a window into the process [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers and exporters, who would bear pre-export notice requirements, labeling costs, and recordkeeping for banned or restricted chemicals. The EPA bears new reporting and notice duties. Costs to domestic farming are minimal, since the listed pesticides (DDT, aldrin, dieldrin, and similar) are already effectively barred from U.S. use.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not automatically ban newly listed chemicals: when an international body proposes listing a pesticide, the EPA may publish a notice, collect comment, and issue a report within 240 days, and any domestic prohibition still must go through an existing registration-cancellation proceeding [S4].

Exporters face new compliance burdens: pre-export notices with detailed content requirements, copies of notices accompanying each shipment, three-year recordkeeping, and labeling and customs-code documentation [S4].
The bill's provisions only apply to the treaties 'if the United States is a party,' so it does nothing on its own unless the Senate consents to ratification of the agreements [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is real but modest in practice: the specific pesticides named (DDT, aldrin, dieldrin, PCBs and similar) are already banned or effectively unavailable in the U.S., so the main gain is export transparency, labeling abroad, and a framework for future listings. The design deliberately avoids automatic domestic bans, requiring EPA review and comment before restrictions, which protects industry from surprise prohibitions but slows protection. The compliance cost falls on exporters of chemicals the U.S. itself will not sell domestically.

outcome.mechanism: The House Agriculture Committee unanimously reported the bill in September 2006 and it was placed on the House calendar, but House leadership never scheduled a floor vote and the Congress ended in January 2007 with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Lucas introduced the bill on September 21, 2005, with three cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S6].
The committee held a hearing on July 20, 2006, ordered the bill reported by voice vote on July 27, and reported it to the House without amendment on September 19, 2006 [S6].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar on September 19, 2006, and no further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended [S6].
The Senate never took up the measure; there is no record of any Senate action or companion bill [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and exporters are better off, since they avoid new export-notice, labeling, and recordkeeping requirements; the treaties also remain unimplemented in U.S. law, leaving the status quo for anyone exposed to exported banned chemicals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide exporters; treaty obligations stayed unimplemented

sides.party_line_note: No recorded opposition exists: the committee reported the bill by voice vote with a Republican sponsor, a Republican cosponsor, and two Democratic cosponsors, and no roll-call vote was ever taken [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill would add export-notification, labeling, and recordkeeping costs for banned or restricted pesticides, but it also shields the industry from automatic domestic bans: new international listings would first require EPA notice, a 240-day report, and comment before any restriction via existing cancellation proceedings. Since the named POPs pesticides are already barred from U.S. use, the domestic status quo is largely preserved.

industries.industry: U.S. pesticide exporters selling unregistered chemicals abroad
industries.note: Exporters of pesticides not registered in the U.S. would face pre-export notices to the EPA and receiving governments plus hazard labeling, a direct cost whose purpose is informing foreign buyers and governments of the risks.
